attempts.label: In Text · p. 558 · question 18
attempts.sourceText: 2   List the key events that happen  to chromosomes in each phase.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: List the key events that happen to chromosomes in each phase.

first_response.prophase: Chromatin condenses into compact replicated chromosomes.
first_response.metaphase: Replicated chromosomes align singly at the equator; sisters are connected toward opposite poles.
first_response.anaphase: Sister chromatids separate, becoming daughter chromosomes that move to opposite poles.
first_response.telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles and decondense; a nuclear envelope forms around each set.

attempts.visible_evidence: pp557–558 and Figure16.8 give the sequence and chromosome behavior.

attempts.label: In Text · p. 559 · question 19
attempts.sourceText: 2   How do mitosis and cytokinesis  differ in plant cells and animal  cells?
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: How do mitosis and cytokinesis differ in plant cells and animal cells?
attempts.first_response: The mitotic chromosome-distribution sequence and spindle microtubules occur in both. Typical animal cells have centrioles; dividing onion/ordinary higher-plant cells lack them but still form spindles. In animal cytokinesis an inward furrow divides the cell; the rigid plant wall does not pinch. Instead, an internal cell plate extends to partition the cell and contributes the new wall.
attempts.visible_evidence: pp558–559; Figure16.9 shows the plant partition. The source generalizes absence of centrioles to all plants; I state its intended onion/higher-plant context.

attempts.label: In Text · p. 563 · question 20
attempts.sourceText: 2   Describe the two key outcomes  of meiosis.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: Describe the two key outcomes of meiosis.
attempts.first_response: Reduction: diploid cells give rise to haploid products with one chromosome set. Recombination: products carry new combinations of genetic information, contributing to genetic variation.
attempts.visible_evidence: p563 lists reduction division and recombination.

attempts.label: In Text · p. 563 · question 21
attempts.sourceText: 2   In what ways does meiosis serve  a different function than mitosis?
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: In what ways does meiosis serve a different function than mitosis?
attempts.first_response: Meiosis supports sexual reproduction by reducing chromosome sets for gamete formation and generating new combinations. Mitosis normally preserves chromosome number/genetic information while supporting growth, maintenance and repair. Fertilization of haploid gametes restores the diploid number.
attempts.visible_evidence: p563 contrasts somatic reproduction and gamete production; p556 gives mitotic functions.

attempts.label: In Text · p. 566 · question 23
attempts.sourceText: 2   Describe the phases of meiosis I  and meiosis II.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: Describe the phases of meiosis I and meiosis II.

first_response.before_division: One S phase replicates the chromosomes before meiosis I. No replication occurs between I and II.
first_response.prophase_I: Replicated homologues pair through synapsis to form tetrads; crossing over between non-sister chromatids can occur.
first_response.metaphase_I: Homologous pairs align at the equator, with the homologues facing opposite poles.
first_response.anaphase_I: Homologues separate, retaining joined sister chromatids.
first_response.telophase_I: Each pole has one homologue of every type. Two haploid groups/cells result; nuclear-envelope/decondensation details vary.
first_response.prophase_II: Within each haploid cell, chromosomes remain replicated and spindle apparatus forms/reorganizes.
first_response.metaphase_II: Replicated chromosomes align singly with sisters directed toward opposite poles.
first_response.anaphase_II: Sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.
first_response.telophase_II: Chromosomes arrive, nuclei reform and cytokinesis yields haploid products with unreplicated chromosomes.

attempts.visible_evidence: pp563–566; complete Figure16.11 on PDF p564 provides the meiosis-II stage sequence as pp565 gives a concise description.

attempts.label: In Text · p. 566 · question 25
attempts.sourceText: 2   Distinguish independent  assortment from crossing over.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: Distinguish independent assortment from crossing over.
attempts.first_response: Independent assortment comes from each homologous pair orienting independently at metaphase I, so whole maternal/paternal homologues are distributed in different combinations. Crossing over is exchange of DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of paired homologues in prophase I, making recombinant chromatids. Both contribute variation through distinct mechanisms.
attempts.visible_evidence: pp565–566; Figures16.13 and16.14 show assortment and segment exchange.

attempts.label: Section 16 2 · p. 561 · question 4
attempts.sourceText: 4. What role does the spindle apparatus play in cell division?
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: What role does the spindle apparatus play in cell division?
attempts.first_response: Its microtubules attach to chromosome-associated structures, position chromosomes at the equator and separate chromosome copies to opposite poles. This distributes a complete chromosome set to each daughter nucleus.

attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: Briefly explain the link between cell cycle regulation and cancer.
attempts.first_response: Regulatory signals normally control when cells divide and stop. Interference with these controls can allow uncontrolled division and tumor formation. Rapid division alone does not establish cancer; the loss of appropriate control is the important link.

 6. The scientists in a lab have isolated a substance that 
prevents cells from synthesizing microtubules. What 
impact would this substance have on cell division? Explain.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: The scientists in a lab have isolated a substance that prevents cells from synthesizing microtubules. What impact would this substance have on cell division? Explain.
attempts.first_response: Cells would be unable to build/maintain the normal spindle adequately, impairing chromosome alignment and separation. Thus normal nuclear division would be blocked or produce errors, rather than reliably delivering a complete set to each daughter. The exact arrest point or residual function depends on when treatment occurs and any microtubules already present.
attempts.visible_evidence: p558 identifies spindle fibres as microtubules, explains growth through added subunits, and connects them to alignment and separation; impact is an inference from that mechanism.
alternatives_and_limits: Does not justify claiming every pre-existing microtubule vanishes immediately or an exact arrest phase without timing/dose information.

 7. A scientist studying a group of somatic cells notices that 
upon the completion of the cell cycle half of the daughter 
cells have no chromosomes and the other half have 
92 chromosomes. In what phase of mitosis did an 
error most likely occur? Explain your reasoning.
attempts.reviewStatus: Original wording retained; geometric crop plus complete source context.
attempts.complete_prompt_transcribed_from_pixels: A scientist studying a group of somatic cells notices that upon the completion of the cell cycle half of the daughter cells have no chromosomes and the other half have 92 chromosomes. In what phase of mitosis did an error most likely occur? Explain your reasoning.
attempts.first_response: Anaphase is the most direct stage implicated: daughter chromosomes should segregate to opposite poles, whereas this outcome suggests all chromosome copies ended up on one side. If the parent was a normal human somatic cell, replication supplied 92 chromatids, which should yield 46 chromosomes to each daughter after separation; the reported 0/92 split is unequal distribution. An earlier spindle-attachment failure could cause the anaphase outcome, and the endpoint alone cannot prove the timing or exclude abnormal cytokinesis.
attempts.visible_evidence: pp557–558 connect anaphase to distribution; the question supplies the 0/92 counts but does not explicitly name the species. Human46 is an explicit contextual assumption, not a given.
alternatives_and_limits: Endpoint does not uniquely identify causal stage. Anaphase is the intended distribution stage; an earlier spindle error or abnormal partition can create a similar outcome. Species is unstated.
